processing: Usually ripe pu-erh combined with a small share of nuo mi xiang (Semnostachya menglaensis), a Yunnan herb that smells of sticky rice, and often pressed into mini tuos. Raw versions are also sold.
harvest_season: Not season-driven; it is a blended product, and the year on the pack refers to the tea or the pressing.
appearance_dry: Small dark brown pressed tuos, bricks or medallions, sometimes with visible herb flecks.
appearance_liquor: Dark reddish brown and opaque in ripe versions, and amber in raw ones.
appearance_wet: Dark ripe leaf mixed with soft pieces of herb.
taste_profile: A clear aroma of cooked sticky rice over the smooth, earthy sweetness of ripe pu-erh; the herb is what gives the rice note, since no rice is involved.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. A mini tuo can also be brewed Western style in a mug with boiling water for a couple of minutes. The aroma is strongest early, so do not expect it to last through a long session.

vintage_note: Sold by pressing year as an everyday tea, usually young and ready to drink. It is not an ageing tea to collect, and the herb's aroma is the point, so buy fresh and keep it sealed.
description:
Nuoxiang Pu-erh tastes of sticky rice but contains none. The aroma comes from nuo mi xiang, a herb that grows in Yunnan, added in a small proportion to the tea. Most of it is ripe pu-erh in small tuos, though the same idea appears in raw tea too.

The herb is usually simply mixed in before pressing, as with other blended pu-erh. Sellers also describe a scented method, where the tea takes up the aroma, in the way jasmine tea does.

The smell is immediate and comforting, on top of a smooth, sweet and earthy base. It is a forgiving tea: use boiling water, keep it short if you dislike a heavy brew, and do not worry about precise timing.

The herb can also hide an ordinary base tea, so this is not the place to judge pu-erh quality. If the rice note seems harsh or artificial, choose another maker and check that the label names the herb.
history:
Little is documented about when pu-erh makers began blending with nuo mi xiang. The herb grows in Yunnan, and the blend is now a common commercial pairing offered by many sellers under names such as nuoxiang and nuo mi xiang.

No inventor or founding recipe is on record.
